title: Landfall Bushwick — Editor Intro
summary: Editorial opening splash: the household reaches assigned shelter after intake; the city calls the case housed before the Vikings have inspected anything, and Carrie is already responsible for whatever they decide the room means.
settingText: Bushwick apartment building stairwell and fifth-floor landing, night
panelPlan: Full-page editorial/title splash. Use the cramped vertical stairwell as the dominant image: Carrie ahead with the brass key and thin DTI folder, the five displaced Norse adults climbing behind with bundled possessions. They should read as an exhausted adventuring party ascending rather than a static line of people on stairs.

Vary the party blocking: one person looking upward, one back down the stairwell, one resting briefly at a landing, Carrie already several steps ahead. The building is ordinary, worn, and much taller than anyone wants it to be.
Leave clean negative-space zones in walls and stairwell voids for the captions. The humor is that municipal paperwork has already declared success while everyone is still climbing.

dialogueInline.text: DTI calls this a successful placement.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION

title: The Fifth-Floor Kingdom
summary: Carrie gets the household to 5B; the climb leaves them tired but alert, and Bjorn and Gunnar immediately judge the apartment as shelter rather than accepting Carrie's description of it.
settingText: Bushwick apartment building stairs and fifth-floor landing
panelPlan: Wide vertical stair composition: the group reaches the final flight looking genuinely weary. Carrie is at the fifth-floor landing with the key; Bjorn and Gunnar are still below her with the Kin distributed across the steps.
Medium at 5B: Carrie unlocks the door while Bjorn remains on the landing looking down the full stairwell they just climbed.
Wide into the studio from the doorway: Astrid and the two male Kin enter with bags while Gunnar stays at the threshold checking the hall, stair direction, and rear window visible beyond.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn at the door: she waits for his verdict; he gives her a logistical one instead of gratitude.
Final medium: Gunnar spots the fire escape through the rear window while Carrie is still trying to get everyone fully inside.

dialogueInline.text: Fifth floor. This is us.
There are four floors beneath us full of strangers.
That's usually how apartment buildings work.
And one stair.
There is a fire escape in back.
I saw it from the alley.
Of course you did.
If the lower stair is held, we leave by the rear iron.
If the building is on fire, yes.
Fire is one reason to leave quickly.
We're going to keep the list at fire.
For tonight.

title: One Room, Six Opinions
summary: The household occupies 5B immediately, making practical choices before Carrie can deliver a tour; Carrie's job becomes stopping only the choices that can damage the building or the placement.
panelPlan: Wide room geography: bare studio, kitchenette, radiator, window/fire escape, limited furniture. The household fans out immediately: Astrid at sink, Kin1 testing floor/wall for bedding, Kin2 testing window latch, Gunnar checking door swing and rear exit, Bjorn standing in the center taking the whole room in.
Medium: Carrie opens the DTI folder to begin her prepared orientation while nobody is facing her.
Medium: Kin1 starts moving a small table away from the wall; Carrie redirects only when it would block the entry door.
Medium: Gunnar tests the fire-escape window latch; Bjorn asks about the roof without looking at Carrie.
Wide: Carrie lowers the folder. The room is already changing around her.

dialogueInline.text: Okay. Before we start moving things—
Door needs the width.
More than that. It opens inward.
Yes. Great. Don't block the door.
Water works.
Window locks.
How do we reach the roof?
You don't.
There is a roof.
There are also sewers. You don't need to inspect the whole city tonight.
The rear window opens onto the iron stair.
Emergency use only.
You keep saying 'only' about useful things.
Because useful things become incident reports when you improvise.

title: The Hidden Fire
summary: Hot water and radiator heat impress the household, but Bjorn's response is suspicion of a system whose critical fire and keeper are somewhere he cannot see; Gunnar immediately wants to inspect it.
panelPlan: Insert: Astrid turns the hot tap; steam begins from the chipped sink.
Medium: Gunnar follows the hot-water pipe with his eyes into the wall and then kneels by the radiator, examining without disassembling it.
Two-shot Bjorn/Carrie: Bjorn stands between sink and radiator, impressed but increasingly suspicious as Carrie names the boiler downstairs.
Medium: Gunnar's hand reaches toward the radiator valve; Carrie catches his wrist or blocks the reach before he touches it.
Wide: The household resumes unpacking while Bjorn keeps looking at the pipe disappearing into the building.

dialogueInline.text: Hot.
From the wall.
Boiler downstairs. Heat and hot water for the building.
One fire serves everyone.
Who keeps it?
The super handles the building. Boiler company if something actually breaks.
So the warmth of the household belongs to a man downstairs and another man we have not met.
It doesn't belong to them.
Can they stop it?
They can. The part you're skipping is that they are paid to keep it running.
The valve is painted shut.
And it is going to enjoy a long, peaceful life exactly like that.
Then tomorrow I want to see the boiler.
Tomorrow you want breakfast.
Both can happen.

title: Emergency Provisions
summary: Carrie's official emergency food bag is revealed to be laughably inadequate for six adults, forcing an immediate neighborhood food run and giving Bjorn his first concrete reason to distrust DTI's idea of being prepared.
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie empties the DTI emergency grocery bag onto the table: crackers, protein bars, bottled water, a few disposable utensils.
Medium on Bjorn looking at the food, then at the five adults around him.
Medium: Gunnar checks the bag itself as though more food may be hidden in a seam.
Medium at window: Gunnar looks down toward storefront awnings and foot traffic below.
Wide: Carrie already has her coat back on as the household prepares to go out.

dialogueInline.text: This is the food they sent with six people?
Five people. I was not included in the nutritional planning.
That improves nothing.
Two bars.
Six crackers.
Water.
Your department provisioned us for a very short siege.
My department provisioned you for a bus ride.
We climbed five floors after the bus ride.
File a grievance with gravity.
Food below us. Bread. Onions. Something frying.
Bodega on the corner. Cash or card.
We have silver.
You have a museum problem. Put your coat on.

title: The Store Downstairs
summary: The first bodega transaction establishes the recurring store, Carrie's financial exposure, and Bjorn's refusal to treat her payment as invisible help.
panelPlan: Wide: all five displaced adults enter the compact bodega with Carrie while ordinary customers continue shopping. The owner looks up once and goes back to work.
Medium: Astrid and the two male Kin choose bread, eggs, fruit and simple food. Gunnar studies shelf prices and package weights rather than staring at products.
Counter close: Bjorn places a small piece of hacksilver beside the groceries.
Two-shot owner/Carrie: the owner looks at the silver and then at Carrie; she already has her card out.
Medium: Carrie pays. Bjorn watches the amount on the terminal and the bagged food.
Close: the owner slides the hacksilver back to Bjorn with the receipt.

dialogueInline.text: Door closes behind you.
For the food.
That's silver.
Cool. I need dollars.
Put it away. I've got it.
I will not have you feeding us as well.
Then tonight's dinner is six crackers and whatever Gunnar can smell from the window.
Onions.
How much?
Fifty-eight forty.
Write it down.
It's groceries, not blood debt.
Then you won't mind writing it down.
Receipt does that.
Good merchant.
Please leave the silver out of it.

title: First Meal
summary: The household cooks without needing a lesson in food or fire; Carrie's only useful contribution is identifying which modern conveniences must not be defeated in the process.
panelPlan: Wide: food preparation underway. Astrid controls the pan; Kin1 cuts bread; Kin2 opens packages; Gunnar works out the unfamiliar stove controls by watching heat response; Bjorn sets out food. Carrie is squeezed to the edge with the DTI folder.
Medium: Carrie starts to explain the stove, then realizes nobody needs a cooking lesson.
Close: Gunnar tests the smoke detector visually from below and notices its position above the kitchenette.
Medium: Bjorn eyes the detector after Gunnar explains what it does.
Wide meal: everyone eats in the still-sparse room while Carrie tries to work.

dialogueInline.text: That knob—
Makes heat. I know.
Fine. Great. I withdraw from dinner.
What is that?
Smoke detector. If there's enough smoke, it screams and the building may evacuate.
It summons everyone because one room has smoke.
It warns everyone. Do not think of it as summoning.
Can it tell cooking smoke from fire smoke?
It detects smoke. It does not know whether dinner caused it.
Primitive.
It has saved more people than either of you.
Then it is primitive and useful.
I'll take it.
Eat before it gets cold.
Finally, an instruction I support.

title: The Iron Stair
summary: Gunnar tests the fire escape and immediately treats the shared exterior as usable terrain; Carrie defines the one thing she actually cares about—egress must remain clear.
settingText: Bushwick studio main window and fire escape
panelPlan: Medium: after dinner Gunnar opens the window and steps onto the fire-escape landing, testing the iron with one boot before putting weight on it.
Wide: Bjorn joins at the window; the Kin remain inside cleaning up. Pigeons occupy the rail and neighboring section.
Medium: Carrie comes over with the DTI folder under one arm and sees Gunnar measuring the landing by stride.
Two-shot Bjorn/Carrie: Bjorn looks down through the iron grid to the alley and then toward neighboring windows.
Close: Gunnar notices pigeons and a clear length of railing.

dialogueInline.text: It holds.
And reaches the ground.
In an emergency. Keep the landing clear.
Clear of what?
Everything. Chairs, boxes, laundry, weapons, projects, livestock—
We have no livestock.
I was trying to get ahead of you.
The birds use it.
The birds don't have a lease.
Then they have even less claim than we do.
That is not where this conversation is going.
Not now.

title: Shared Space
summary: Carrie discovers Gunnar has already converted 'shared fire escape' into 'unclaimed hunting ground'; she stops the snare because it blocks emergency egress, not because the Vikings need a lesson about birds.
settingText: Bushwick fire escape and apartment window
panelPlan: Wide: a simple cord snare on the fire escape has caught one ordinary pigeon by the leg without injuring it. Gunnar crouches beside it; Bjorn has brought a bowl inside the window as if dinner logistics are already underway.
Medium: Carrie returns from the table holding her phone and sees the bird, cord, bowl, and two men in one look.
Close: Gunnar loosens the snare while explaining his reasoning; the pigeon remains alive and calm enough to be released.
Medium: Carrie points to the cord crossing part of the shared landing and the drop ladder path.
Wide: Gunnar releases the pigeon and gathers the cord. Bjorn watches the bird fly away with genuine disappointment.

dialogueInline.text: The fire escape is not a pantry.
It wasn't in the apartment.
That sentence is somehow worse.
The bird belongs to no one.
I don't care about the bird.
You came over very quickly for someone who doesn't care about the bird.
I care about the cord across the only legal emergency exit in an apartment I personally signed you into six hours ago.
The cord caught the bird.
The cord can also catch Mrs. Whoever-Lives-Next-Door while the building is on fire.
Then we move the snare farther from her window.
We remove the snare from the fire escape.
You have chosen the bird over us.
I have chosen not explaining 'Viking pigeon trap' to Housing.
That is not the same reason.
It's the reason that wins.

title: The Neighbor Has the Cord
summary: The upstairs neighbor arrives with the loose end of Gunnar's cord and no interest in anyone's cultural development; Astrid settles the immediate friction with food while Carrie realizes the incident has already escaped the apartment.
panelPlan: Wide: knock at 5B. Upstairs Neighbor stands in the hall holding a length of cord that crossed her portion of the fire escape. Carrie opens the door; Bjorn is immediately behind her.
Medium: Neighbor holds the cord out to Carrie, irritated rather than frightened.
Medium: Carrie starts a formal apology; Astrid appears beside Bjorn with one unopened packaged snack from the bodega.
Close: Astrid offers the snack; Neighbor takes it after a beat without becoming friendly.
Wide: Neighbor walks away. Carrie closes the door while Bjorn watches the hallway.

dialogueInline.text: This yours?
Yes. It is no longer doing what it was doing.
It was tied across my fire escape.
The boundary was unclear.
The boundary is my window.
Clear now.
I'm sorry. It won't happen again.
For trouble.
What is it?
Spicy.
Fine.
Keep whatever you tied off my window.
Jesus Christ.
What were you doing out there?
Catching a pigeon.

title: The Signature Problem
summary: Carrie returns to the required placement acknowledgement; Bjorn refuses to make a conventional signature because he cannot read the statement it would certify, turning a routine form into a real problem for Carrie's file.
panelPlan: Wide: night deeper outside. The household continues organizing bedding and food while Carrie clears a corner of the table and places the placement acknowledgement in front of Bjorn.
Insert: signature line and acknowledgement language.
Medium: Carrie offers the pen. Bjorn does not touch it.
Two-shot: Bjorn points at the paragraph above the line; Carrie realizes the refusal is specific, not stubbornness.
Medium: Gunnar sits nearby repairing/recoiling the confiscated fire-escape cord and listens.

dialogueInline.text: I need this signed before I can close the placement.
Read it.
I already explained the rules.
Then read what I am marking.
It says you acknowledge the placement conditions, received the safety information, understand the temporary status—
There. 'Understand.' That's the word.
What about it?
Because if I make my name there, you will keep the page. Later someone will say I knew what the page said because my name is on it.
That's basically what a signature does.
I cannot read it.
Then his name would prove something untrue.
That's the problem.
Good. We have found the bad part.
We have found the part that keeps me here.

title: A Mark Is Not Reading
summary: Gunnar reframes the problem around witnessing Bjorn's agreement rather than manufacturing literacy; Carrie realizes DTI may already have a lawful mechanism for exactly that.
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie writes BJORN on scrap paper and then stops before sliding it toward him, recognizing the obvious workaround is false.
Medium: Gunnar rotates the acknowledgement and studies the signature area without pretending to read it.
Two-shot Gunnar/Bjorn: Gunnar describes how a mark can identify a person without claiming the person read the writing.
Close on Carrie searching the DTI guidance on her phone/laptop while they continue talking.
Insert on guidance search results or footnote language: witnessed mark / unable to execute conventional signature.

dialogueInline.text: I could show you how to copy your name.
Then I would become a man who can copy his name.
Right. Not a man who can read the form.
He has marks.
What kind of marks?
His. On trade. On promises. On things everyone present understands.
A mark is not the words. The witness carries the words.
Then my signature carries the words. That is more responsibility than I wanted tonight.
You already read it to him.
Which means if DTI has a witnessed-mark procedure, I can document exactly what happened instead of faking what didn't.
Then use the mark.
Nobody move. I may have found something written by a competent adult.

title: Strongly Prefers
summary: Carrie invokes DTI's witnessed-mark exception; the supervisor resists out of preference rather than law, and Bjorn immediately recognizes a hierarchy in which the written rule outranks the person administering it.
settingText: Bushwick studio table / phone on speaker
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie's phone on speaker beside the open acknowledgement and guidance footnote.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn: she points to the written exception while arguing with the supervisor.
Close on phone/screen and Carrie's finger at REQUIRED versus PREFERRED language.
Medium on Bjorn listening with increasing interest as the supervisor concedes.
Medium: Carrie hangs up; Bjorn looks pleased for an entirely different reason than she does.

dialogueInline.text: I have an applicant who understood the terms and cannot execute a conventional signature. The guidance allows a witnessed mark.
We strongly prefer a conventional signature.
I strongly prefer a lot of things. Is it required?
You know why we prefer the standard signature.
I know what you prefer. Is it required?
It is not required.
Then I'm using the witnessed mark.
The book defeated him.
The policy clarified the procedure.
He wanted one thing. The written law said another. The law won.
She used his own book.
Then the book outranks the man holding it.
I just taught you that my department can be overruled by its own paperwork.
I will remember that.

title: Witnessed
summary: Bjorn uses a thumbprint as a truthful mark, then immediately asks what binds the other side of the housing agreement; the solution to Carrie's paperwork problem gives him a much larger opinion about tenancy.
panelPlan: Insert: black ink pad, witnessed-mark box, Carrie's pen, acknowledgement.
Close: Bjorn presses his thumb into the ink and makes the mark deliberately.
Medium: Carrie signs the witness field while Bjorn watches her write.
Two-shot: Bjorn asks where the landlord's obligations are recorded; Carrie reaches for the lease/placement packet.
Close: Bjorn studies the landlord signature/printed obligations he cannot read but now knows exist.

dialogueInline.text: No blood?
Ink. We are going to have one normal procedural victory tonight.
You witness that I agreed to what you read.
That's what my signature says.
And you put your own name beside mine.
Right under yours.
Good. Now show me where the owner agrees.
The landlord?
The man who owns the walls, roof and furnace and takes payment for our use of them.
Yes. The landlord.
You say that word as though it helps your argument.
Land. Lord.
That is etymology, not tenancy law.
It split itself.

title: Provisional
summary: DTI accepts the witnessed mark and provisional placement, but the night's fire-escape incident has already generated a separate building complaint tied to Carrie's case.
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie photographs/scans and submits the witnessed form.
Insert: DTI confirmation: conditional/provisional placement accepted; review pending.
Wide: household has already arranged food, bedding, tools and clear exit paths in the sparse room.
Medium: Carrie's phone immediately rings again before she can celebrate.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn: she listens; Bjorn can hear enough of the call to recognize the fire escape is now part of the official record.

dialogueInline.text: Conditional placement accepted. Review remains pending.
Great. Thank you.
We can stay.
You can stay.
Separate issue.
Of course there is.
Building management forwarded a complaint about an obstruction on the rear fire escape.
Removed. Immediately. No injury, no damage.
The note says 'animal snare.'
Successful animal snare.
Nobody asked you.
Was that him?
I am going to say no until I decide what makes my life worse.

title: The Brass Key
summary: Carrie hands over the single apartment key; Bjorn understands the lock immediately and values the privacy far more than the paperwork that produced it.
panelPlan: Insert: scratched brass key in Carrie's palm.
Close: Bjorn takes it and turns it once between thumb and forefinger.
Two-shot at the door: Carrie demonstrates the deadbolt only as much as needed; Bjorn tests the lock himself.
Medium: Gunnar points out that one key is a bottleneck for six adults.
Close: Bjorn closes his hand around the key.

dialogueInline.text: One key tonight. Copies tomorrow.
One key for six people is a poor arrangement.
For once, your complaint is completely normal.
From inside, the door answers to us.
Once it's locked, the door answers to you.
And from outside, the key decides.
That's a lock.
An excellent invention.
Until the person with the only key leaves.
Tomorrow we make six.
Tomorrow a locksmith makes copies. You make nothing.
Then tomorrow the locksmith proves useful.

directionInline.text: Use the same ordinary scratched brass apartment key established throughout the issue.

title: The Landlord
summary: Carrie explains only enough of rent to establish mutual obligations; Bjorn immediately concludes that the landlord is functionally a lord and refuses Carrie's insistence that modern vocabulary changes the relationship.
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie writes the first rent due date on a scrap beside the lease/placement packet.
Two-shot: Bjorn holds the brass key and listens while Carrie points to heat, water, roof and lock as landlord obligations.
Medium: Gunnar begins making a two-column tally of what the household owes and what the building owes.
Close on Bjorn reaching his conclusion with total seriousness.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn: she realizes the explanation has made his opinion worse, not better.

dialogueInline.text: Placement gets you in. Rent keeps the tenancy going.
We pay the man who owns the building.
That's the arrangement.
And he owes you heat, water, a sound roof, working locks, repairs—
I'll keep a tally of what we owe and what he owes.
Call it receipts if anyone official asks.
He owns the walls.
He owns the building.
He owns the roof.
He controls the hidden fire.
The boiler is not a feudal office.
And we pay him to remain on his land.
Property. We pay rent for the apartment.
He is our lord.
He is absolutely not your lord.
I have considered your explanation.
You considered it for three seconds.
It was sufficient.

title: Their Order
summary: The household arranges 5B according to its own practical priorities; Carrie stops a single genuinely dangerous use of building equipment and otherwise lets them make the room strange on their own terms.
panelPlan: Wide: Astrid claims food/cooking shelf; Kin1 selects dry bedding area; Kin2 arranges small tools; Gunnar preserves exit paths; Bjorn tries to reserve a central patch for shared gear.
Medium: Kin1 ignores Bjorn's preferred bedding placement and moves his own bundle back.
Medium: Kin2 starts hanging a heavy wet item from a sprinkler pipe because it is conveniently placed.
Fast intervention: Carrie crosses the room and removes it before anyone argues.
Wide: the rest of the arrangement continues without central command.

dialogueInline.text: Shared gear stays here. Bedding along that wall.
No. Draft.
It is six feet from where I said.
Still draft.
Not on the sprinkler.
Strong pipe.
Connected to enough water to destroy everything you own.
Useful.
Only when the building is on fire.
Another useful thing with one approved purpose.
Yes. New York is full of them.
Food here.
Door stays clear.
And nobody touches the lord's water spear.
I regret explaining rent.

title: The Radiator Knocks
summary: The radiator's harmless knocking confirms that the hidden heat system works but also makes Bjorn and Gunnar more interested in the unseen machinery, not more reassured by it.
panelPlan: Insert: old cast-iron radiator gives a loud metallic knock under hard practical light.
Medium: Gunnar crouches immediately, listening to the pipe and feeling heat near the radiator without touching the valve.
Two-shot Carrie/Gunnar: she identifies ordinary radiator knock; he asks about the basement access.
Medium on Bjorn warming his hands, genuinely impressed by the heat while still suspicious of its distance.
Wide: everyone returns to tasks except Bjorn and Gunnar, who remain focused on the pipe disappearing through the floor.

dialogueInline.text: There. Again.
Radiator knock. Annoying, normal, not dying.
Where does the pipe go?
Basement.
Can we get into the basement?
Not through any door you're authorized to open.
Locked?
Locked, and not part of this apartment.
Then something important is in there.
That is not a universal law.
It is warm enough to sleep beside.
See? A compliment.
I compliment the heat. I have not met the men responsible for it.
You do not need to inspect the boiler staff.
Then tomorrow I want to meet the man responsible for the heat.
Tomorrow you are not going into the basement.
Then he can come upstairs.

title: Who Do We Call
summary: Carrie leaves contact numbers; Gunnar reorganizes them into a practical hierarchy that is accurate enough to be useful and strange enough that Carrie forbids it from entering official paperwork.
settingText: Bushwick studio table near the door
panelPlan: Insert: Carrie writes building super, DTI after-hours, her office number, 311, and 911 on a card.
Medium: Gunnar copies the numbers onto his small household map with short labels of his own.
Close on Gunnar's labels as Carrie reads them over his shoulder.
Two-shot: Bjorn contributes his interpretation of the chain of authority.
Medium: Carrie takes the original contact card away from Gunnar and puts it beside the door where everyone can find it.

dialogueInline.text: Building problem: super. DTI problem: after-hours. Emergency: 911. City problem that is not an emergency: 311.
Super: steward.
Close enough for the map.
Three-one-one: complaint hall.
Not what it's called.
Nine-one-one: armed help.
Police, fire, ambulance.
Armed help, fire help, blood help.
I am begging you not to submit this map to anyone.
And DTI?
For us, DTI has mostly been you.
DTI is not me.
Tonight it has been mostly you.
That sentence is going to follow me into a disciplinary hearing.
Disciplinary hearing.
Do not add it to the map.

title: Incident Report
summary: Carrie's successful placement immediately produces a required incident report for the fire-escape snare; Bjorn and Gunnar are offended that the official record is less precise than their version of events.
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie sits at the table filling a DTI incident form on phone/laptop while the household settles the room around her.
Insert: incident category includes FIRE ESCAPE OBSTRUCTION / ANIMAL TRAP or equivalent neutral administrative wording.
Medium: Gunnar reads over Carrie's shoulder despite not being invited; Bjorn listens from nearby.
Two-shot: Carrie corrects their attempts to improve the report.
Wide: Carrie keeps typing while the rest of the room prepares for sleep.

dialogueInline.text: You wrote 'snare removed.'
Because the snare was removed.
It does not say it caught anything.
That is not a deficiency.
An unsuccessful snare and a successful snare are different facts.
The fact DTI cares about is that there was a snare on a fire escape.
Then why ask for details?
Because bureaucracy is a machine that becomes hungry when you feed it.
You should not feed a dangerous machine.
I know. I work there.
Write that the bird was unharmed.
It already says the bird was unharmed.
And well fed.
It stole half an apple after you released it. That is not part of the incident.
Your records lack texture.

title: Carrie's Excellent Placement
summary: The DTI supervisor calls about the incident; Carrie defends the placement as safe and corrected while the Vikings' audible commentary makes her case progressively harder to present as routine.
panelPlan: Medium: phone on speaker, Carrie seated at table with completed placement paperwork and incident report.
Medium on Carrie as supervisor lists the complaint facts in bureaucratic language.
Medium on Bjorn and Gunnar nearby, listening as though this is a review of their work.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn as she tries to keep him out of the call.
Close on Carrie after the supervisor reminds her the placement is under her supervision.

dialogueInline.text: First night: obstruction of required egress, animal trapping, neighbor complaint.
Corrected before the complaint reached us. No injury. No damage. Egress is clear.
You were on site.
I was standing three feet from it.
The placement is under your supervision.
I am aware of the sentence you are building.
Tell him the neighbor accepted compensation.
She accepted a spicy snack.
Compensation.
Was that him again?
I have five adults in one room and no private office. Everybody is 'him again.'
One more building-safety complaint and Housing can request reassessment.
Then I'll keep Housing out of it.
We also understand.
You understand nothing until I hang up.

title: Tomorrow's Orders
summary: Carrie lays down a compressed list of things that must not happen before morning; Bjorn treats the length of the list as evidence of how productive the evening has been, while Gunnar notices the one place Carrie forgot to forbid.
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie stands near the door putting on her coat; household now functional but still sparse.
Medium: Carrie gives the shortest possible overnight prohibition list while Bjorn holds the brass key.
Reaction on Gunnar as Carrie names fire escape, plumbing, boiler, sprinkler and weapons.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn: he observes the list has grown rapidly.
Close on Gunnar looking upward toward the ceiling after Carrie finishes.

dialogueInline.text: Until I come back: no hunting from the building, no tying anything to the fire escape, no opening walls, no touching the radiator valves, no basement, no sprinkler pipes, and if somebody knocks, answer the door without a weapon in your hand.
You made a long law from a short evening.
You gave me excellent source material.
The bird was one event.
The bird is going in my performance review.
You did not say roof.
I am saying roof now.
You said no basement.
No roof.
I heard the new rule.
We can inspect it tomorrow?
Tomorrow I will explain why I still have a job.

title: Lock It Behind Me
summary: Carrie finally leaves; the key gives the household privacy, but the last exchange makes clear she is not leaving them wiser—only temporarily contained.
settingText: Bushwick studio doorway and fifth-floor hallway
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie stands in open doorway with coat and folder; household remains inside among bedding, groceries, tools and map.
Medium: Bjorn follows to threshold with brass key.
Close: Carrie points to the key and then the lock.
Hallway two-shot: she steps outside; Bjorn remains inside.
Insert from inside: brass key turns, deadbolt locks.
Wide interior: Bjorn tests the handle. Gunnar sits with the map, already looking upward; the others continue settling.

dialogueInline.text: Lock the door behind me.
You cannot enter without the key.
That is the dream.
You are responsible for us but cannot enter our room.
That's how privacy works.
Your government has finally produced a sensible arrangement.
Good night, Bjorn.
Good night, Carrie.
She forgot the window.
She said no fire escape.
I said window.

dialogueInline.text: Food is up.
Bedding is dry.
Window holds.
Door locks. Heat works. Water works.
We have seen them work for one evening.
Which is why tomorrow we inspect what keeps them working.
Roof tomorrow.
North first.
Roof makes north easier.
Sleep makes both easier.
Oh, come on.
